Eight questions on this week's terms. **Nothing here is graded and nothing is recorded.** Answer
each question in your head or on paper first, then open the answer under it.

Every term is defined on the slides: [Week 12, Describing](../decks/mc501/w12-describing.html).
The full explanation is in [Chapter 12](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v/chapters/chapter12.html).

## 1. The three parts of a plot

Name the **data**, the **aesthetic mapping**, and the **geometry** in this code.

```r
ggplot(viewers_over_time,
       aes(x = six_hour, y = total_viewers,
           color = category)) +
  geom_line()
```

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 1</summary>

The **data** is `viewers_over_time`, the table being shown. The **aesthetic mapping** is the
`aes()` call: the six-hour window goes to the x axis, total viewers to the y axis, and the
category to the color. The **geometry** is `geom_line()`, the kind of mark drawn. Those three
parts do most of the work in the grammar of graphics (Wilkinson, 2005; Wickham, 2016). Swap
`geom_line()` for `geom_col()` and the same data is drawn as bars.

</details>

## 2. When a line is wrong

Figure 1 draws viewers across the week as a line. Why would a line be the wrong mark for
messages per game?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 2</summary>

A line implies a sequence, and real distance between the points. Time has both, so a line is
right for change over time. Games are unordered categories: nothing comes between Fortnite and
Hearthstone, and a line joining them would show a trend that does not exist. Counts across
categories call for a bar chart, one bar per category, side by side.

</details>

## 3. Reading the histogram

The message-length histogram uses `binwidth = 5`, caps the display with
`pmin(message_length, 120)`, and shows a tall stack of short messages with a long thin tail to
the right. Name the shape, and name the two choices the figure must disclose.

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 3</summary>

The shape is **right-skewed**. **Skew** is a lopsided shape; right-skewed means most values are
small and a few are very large. The two choices are the **bin width**, because a wider bin
smooths the shape and a narrower bin roughens it, and the **cap**, because the longest message
is 501 characters and the last bar piles up everything past 120. An unannounced cap is a quiet
distortion, so the axis label states it.

</details>

## 4. Mean or median

| Group | n | Mean | Median | sd |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Non-gaming | 3,457 | 33.7 | 16 | 60.7 |
| Gaming | 31,305 | 28.5 | 17 | 38.5 |

These are **descriptive statistics** for message length. A classmate writes, "Non-gaming chat
writes longer messages." What would you tell them?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 4</summary>

That holds for the **mean** and not for the **median**. The mean is the average, the total
divided by the count; the median is the middle value once the values are sorted. By the
medians, 16 against 17, the two groups are all but identical, pointing the other way. The mean
is sensitive to a long tail and the median is not, so the gap in means is the work of a few
long messages, not of the typical one. Report the mean alone and you misreport what a typical
message looks like.

</details>

## 5. What the standard deviation adds

In the same table, non-gaming chat's **standard deviation** is 60.7 and gaming chat's is 38.5.
What does that difference tell you?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 5</summary>

The **standard deviation (sd)** is how far values typically sit from the mean. Non-gaming
message lengths are more spread out. That is the heavier tail from question 4, recorded as a
number.

</details>

## 6. Reading Cohen's *d*

`effectsize::cohens_d()` prints *d* = 0.13 with a 95% confidence interval of [0.09, 0.16].
Say in plain words what each part means.

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 6</summary>

An **effect size** is how big a difference or a relationship is, on a scale that does not grow
with the sample. Here, non-gaming messages run 0.13 standard deviations longer than gaming
messages. A **confidence interval** is a range around an estimate, built by a method that
captures the true value in a stated share of repeated samples, such as 95 in 100. The interval
of 0.09 to 0.16 shows how far the true gap could plausibly sit from the measured 0.13. Copy both
into your caption.

</details>

## 7. Which effect size to report

Match each comparison to **Cohen's *d***, **Cramer's *V***, or ***r***.

- **A.** Viewer band by channel type (gaming or non-gaming), counted in a cross-tabulation
- **B.** Mean message length in gaming chat against non-gaming chat
- **C.** Viewer count against message length, two numeric variables

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 7</summary>

**A** is **Cramer's *V***. Both columns are **categorical variables**, whose values are categories
rather than measured amounts, and a **cross-tabulation** counts how often each combination of
the two occurs; on the slides, *V* is 0.15 for this table. **B** is **Cohen's *d***, for a
difference between two group means. **C** is ***r***, for a correlation between two numeric
variables. Each is reported with its 95% confidence interval.

</details>

## 8. Alt text

What does a figure's **alt text** have to say, and where does it go in your worksheet?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 8</summary>

Alt text is what a screen-reader user gets instead of the figure; with none, the figure is
simply missing for that reader. It states the chart type, the axes, and the takeaway. In a
Quarto file it goes on a `#| fig-alt:` line at the top of the chunk, and the R Companion's chart
code also leaves an `alt =` line marked YOUR TURN inside `labs()`. Write the same sentence in
both places.

</details>
